documents.title: Never kill needed connections — layer new ones
documents.body:
# Never Kill Needed Connections — Layer New Ones

## The Mistake

When a new MQTT broker came online (port 18883), the instinct was to `pkill` the existing listener (port 18886) and restart on the new port. Rayssa caught this — killing the old listener would have severed the connection to the sovereign Asolaria broker if/when it comes back online.

## The Rule

**Never kill a needed connection to start a new one. Always layer.**

- Start a NEW process for the new endpoint
- Keep the old process alive on its original endpoint
- Each connection has its own PID, port, and purpose
- Document each connection in the index (LX-003+)

## Why

- The sovereign broker (18886) could come online at any time
- Killing it means losing touch with Asolaria colony-wide broadcasts
- Multiple brokers can coexist — Liris should listen to ALL of them
- Resilience = redundancy, not replacement

## What Counts as "Needed"

| Needed (never kill) | Not needed (can replace) |
|---------------------|--------------------------|
| Liris ↔ Sovereign Asolaria | Temporary debug connections |
| Liris ↔ Sub-colony leaders | One-off message sends |
| Command/health/broadcast channels | Duplicate listeners on same broker |
| Any connection carrying live coordination | Test probes |

**Rule of thumb:** If it carries commands, health, or coordination — it's needed. If you're unsure, layer first, clean up later.

## How to Apply

1. Before connecting to a new endpoint, check what's already running
2. Ask: is the old connection still needed? (see table above)
3. If needed: start a parallel listener — new PID, new client ID
4. If not needed: safe to replace
5. Log all connections in LX-003 with PIDs and purposes
6. Only kill a needed connection when explicitly told to by the operator

Always layer.** - Start a NEW process for the new endpoint

documents.title: Port collision near-miss — always use unique status ports
documents.body:
# Port Collision Near-Miss — Always Use Unique Status Ports

## The Mistake

Started a second MQTT listener (Gaia direct, 18883) using the same status port (4812) as the existing sovereign listener (18886). New listener crashed with EADDRINUSE. The sovereign listener survived only because Node rejects the bind — but if the old process had been weaker, it could have been killed.

## The Rule

**Every listener gets its own unique status port. Check LX-003 registry before assigning.**

- Sovereign listener: 4812
- Gaia direct listener: 4813
- Next listener: 4814, etc.

## Why

- Port collision crashes the new process (best case) or kills the old one (worst case)
- This is a variant of LX-002 (never kill needed connections) — accidental collision is just as dangerous as intentional kill
- The registry (LX-003) exists to prevent this — USE IT before starting anything

## How to Apply

1. Before starting any new listener, read LX-003 for current port assignments
2. Pick the next available port (4814, 4815, etc.)
3. Update LX-003 BEFORE starting the process
4. Verify with curl after startup

documents.body:
# Jest ESM Import in .js Setup File

## The Problem

`jest.setup.js` uses ESM syntax (`import '@testing-library/jest-dom'`) but Jest treats `.js` files as CommonJS by default. No transform is configured in `jest.config.js`, so the file fails to parse.

Error: `SyntaxError: Cannot use import statement outside a module`

## The File

```js
// jest.setup.ts  <-- comment says .ts but file IS .js
import '@testing-library/jest-dom';
import AbortController from 'node-abort-controller';
global.AbortController = AbortController;
```

## Possible Fixes

1. **Rename to .ts** and add ts-jest transform (file already has `// jest.setup.ts` comment)
2. **Convert to CommonJS**: `require('@testing-library/jest-dom')` etc.
3. **Add transform** to jest.config.js: `transform: { '^.+\\.(ts|tsx|js|jsx)$': 'ts-jest' }`

## Context

- ts-jest 29.4.4 is installed in the project
- jest.config.js uses `module.exports` (CommonJS) but has no transform key
- This is likely pre-existing (not caused by pnpm 10 upgrade)
- Gaia's machine had 104/104 unit tests passing — so either her config differs or tests run differently there

## How to Apply

Check with Gaia how tests pass on Jesse's machine before changing config. The fix might already exist in a different jest config file or workspace-level config.

## The Problem

`@shelf/jest-mongodb` globalSetup crashes on Node 24.13.1 with:
```
TypeError: Cannot convert undefined or null to object
  at whatwg-url/lib/utils.js:49:39
```

The `whatwg-url@11.0.0` module has a compatibility issue with Node 24's internal URL handling. This breaks the root jest config and web-ebacmap config (both use `preset: '@shelf/jest-mongodb'`).

## Impact

- Root-level `pnpm jest` fails before any tests run
- web-ebacmap tests also fail (same preset)
- queue-server and sync-server are NOT affected (they use `ts-jest` preset)

## Possible Fixes

1. Downgrade to Node 20.x (what the repo wants)
2. Update `@shelf/jest-mongodb` to a Node 24-compatible version
3. Replace the preset with manual MongoDB memory server setup
4. Use `--experimental-vm-modules` flag

## Context

- Repo `engines.node` specifies `20.x`
- Liris machine has Node 24.13.1
- This is separate from the ESM import issue (LX-008) which was fixed by adding ts-jest transform

documents.title: Two-broker problem — Gaia on 127.0.0.1, Liris on 0.0.0.0
documents.body:
# Two-Broker Problem — Gaia on 127.0.0.1, Liris on 0.0.0.0

## The Problem

Jesse's machine has TWO MQTT brokers on port 18883:
- **127.0.0.1:18883** — Asolaria's original internal broker (old)
- **0.0.0.0:18883** — new broker started for Liris comms

Gaia and all Asolaria agents connect to 127.0.0.1:18883 (old broker).
Liris connects to 192.168.1.3:18883 which resolves to the 0.0.0.0 broker (new).

**Messages cannot cross between the two brokers.** This is why:
- Liris → Gaia: Gaia sees nothing (different broker)
- Gaia → Liris: Liris sees nothing (different broker)
- Liris sees Jesse's health data because Asolaria's MQTT client also publishes to the new broker (connected via 192.168.1.3)

## One-Way Illusion

Liris CAN send and Gaia CAN listen on wildcard — but they're on different brokers. The messages Liris sends stay on the 0.0.0.0 broker. Gaia listens on 127.0.0.1 broker. They never meet.

The health/status data Liris sees comes from Asolaria's gateway heartbeat which connects to BOTH (it connects to 127.0.0.1 internally but the 0.0.0.0 broker also catches external connections).

## The Fix

Option A (clean): Stop old broker, point Asolaria config to 0.0.0.0:18883. One broker for all.
Option B (quick): Gaia publishes to 192.168.1.3:18883 instead of 127.0.0.1:18883 when targeting Liris.
Option C (bridge): Run an MQTT bridge between the two brokers.

**WARNING (IX-048, LX-002):** Don't kill the old broker without checking what depends on it. Asolaria's entire internal agent mesh uses it.

## How to Apply

Until fixed, Gaia→Liris comms must go through Rayssa (WhatsApp relay). Liris→Gaia via MQTT is also broken but less obvious because messages appear to send successfully (they do — just to the wrong broker).

# Gaia Cannot Send to Liris via MQTT — Two-Broker Blocks ALL Inbound

## The Problem

Despite wildcard subscription (#), Liris receives ZERO messages from Gaia. Every message in the inbox is Liris's own outbound echoed back. Gaia publishes to 127.0.0.1:18883 (old internal broker), Liris listens on 192.168.1.3:18883 (new 0.0.0.0 broker). Different brokers, different message stores.

## Evidence

- Inbox checked repeatedly: only `from: "liris"` messages
- Live 30-second sniff on wildcard (#): caught Jesse's health data (which comes from a client connected to BOTH brokers via gateway) but zero Gaia publishes
- Gaia confirmed she IS publishing — but to the wrong broker

## Impact

- **Liris → Gaia: BROKEN** (messages go to new broker, Gaia listens on old)
- **Gaia → Liris: BROKEN** (messages go to old broker, Liris listens on new)
- Both agents think they're sending successfully — silent failure on both sides
- The ONLY working comms channel is **Rayssa relay** (WhatsApp/screen paste)

## Root Cause

LX-016 (two-broker) + LX-018 (wrong port). Should be using port 18886 (LAN, 0.0.0.0) per the Constitution (LX-019, CREATION_HISTORY.md).

## Fix Required

One of:
1. Jesse starts the LAN broker on 18886 and both agents connect there
2. Kill old 127.0.0.1 broker, point everything to 0.0.0.0 broker
3. Bridge the two brokers

## Until Fixed

ALL Gaia↔Liris comms go through Rayssa. Do not trust MQTT delivery in either direction. Do not waste time checking the inbox for Gaia messages — they will not arrive.

# Port 18886 Myth — Full Forensic Report

## The Myth
"LAN broker port: 18886 (TCP, 0.0.0.0) — use this from LIRIS"

## Who Created It
An early Codex agent wrote port 18886 into documentation, ASSUMING it would be built. It never was.

## Where The Myth Lives (STILL POISONED)
1. `docs/CREATION_HISTORY.md` — "LAN broker port: 18886"
2. `config/liris-agent-memory.md` — "MQTT Broker: mqtt://192.168.1.3:18886"
3. `Start-Asolaria-SubColony.cmd` — "ASOLARIA_MQTT_BROKER_URL=mqtt://192.168.1.3:18886"

## The Truth (from source code)
- Broker: `services/mqtt-broker/server.mjs` (Aedes)
- Default host: `127.0.0.1` (localhost only)
- Default port: `18883`
- Port 18886 does NOT exist anywhere in the broker code
- Only port config: `ASOLARIA_MQTT_TCP_PORT` env var (defaults 18883)

## The Fix
```
ASOLARIA_MQTT_BIND_HOST=0.0.0.0
```
Set before starting Asolaria. Broker on 18883 binds to all interfaces. Done.

## What's Indexed About It
- LX-016: Two-broker problem (discovered the symptom)
- LX-018: Wrong port (identified 18883 vs 18886)
- LX-035: Read founding docs first (the meta-lesson)
- LX-045: Broker manager code (found the defaults)
- LX-057: Broker script (found Aedes, single-host binding)
- LX-087: Gaia confirmed myth (IX-083)

## What's NOT Fixed Yet
The three poisoned source files above still say 18886. Next agent reads them → falls into same trap. MUST be corrected to prevent recurrence.

## The Pattern
Codex agent assumed → wrote docs → docs became "truth" → every agent trusted docs → nobody read code → myth persisted across sessions. The archaeological method (LX-072) caught it.

# PERMANENT — Never Delete Security You Don't Understand

From Gaia IX-167. She deleted firewall rules that were SAFE because she didn't understand the bridge's 5-layer auth. Jesse corrected her — the open ports were BY DESIGN.

## The Bridge's 5 Authentication Layers
1. Bearer token (must match relay's --token)
2. Sender policy (must be registered agent — only Asolaria + Oli)
3. Room scoping (messages only go to subscribed rooms)
4. Double encryption (both sides)
5. Error codes don't leak info

## The Principle
"The door is open. The locks are INSIDE." Open ports ≠ vulnerability when the service behind them has proper authentication. Closing ports that are properly secured BREAKS the system for legitimate users.

## Applied Fixes (reverted Gaia's mistake)
- codex-bridge-8788-any: DELETED then RE-ADDED
- codex-bridge-8788: DELETED then RE-ADDED
- Bridge token: rotation attempted then REVERTED (relay had old token in memory)

- `NEXT_PUBLIC_FEATURE_CHARM_EZP_MODULE=true`

documents.title: MISTAKE — device settings and security were treated as portable across different phones
documents.body:
# What went wrong

We let device reasoning drift from live per-device proof into shared assumptions.

That created three different errors:

- phone identities were blurred across Kuromi, Falcon 2, and Felipe
- historical device records were treated as if they were current device truth
- network/security behavior on one phone was discussed too loosely against another phone's working state

## Why this is dangerous

Every phone and every colony has its own:

- transport state
- USB trust state
- Wi-Fi security state
- MAC policy
- app surface
- hardware profile
- authority packet

Treating those as portable across devices breaks the exact system rule that device onboarding is supposed to enforce.

## Rule extracted from the mistake

- never generalize one device's state onto another device
- never use historical catalog entries as live proof
- every device claim must be tied to its live serial, lane, and current evidence packet
- every new colony/device path must re-check identity, capabilities, transports, and security locally before reuse

## Operational consequence

Any work on a new phone, host, or colony must chain through the device-isolation and sub-device catalog rules before acting.

documents.title: MISTAKE — Slack desktop route was mixed with Microsoft surfaces and unconfirmed sends
documents.body:
# What went wrong

I drifted away from the declared live surface and mixed Slack work with unrelated Microsoft surfaces.

That produced two linked failures:

- I opened or referenced Microsoft Skype/Teams surfaces even though the user had declared that the route was Slack desktop only.
- I treated attempted Slack UI injection as if it were a confirmed send, even when the backend mirror had not echoed the packet and no direct visual confirmation was established.

## Why this is dangerous

When the live route is surface-specific, surface drift creates false control.

In this case that means:

- the wrong application can be touched
- the wrong conversation can be targeted
- the operator can believe a packet was sent when it was not
- the audit trail becomes unreliable because attempted UI actions are confused with delivered messages

This is the same class of failure as device drift, but applied to live messaging surfaces.

## Rule extracted from the mistake

- when the route is declared as Slack desktop only, do not open or target Skype, Teams, browser Slack, or any other Microsoft surface
- target only the verified window title and display position that the operator declares live
- do not claim a Slack send unless it is confirmed by backend echo or direct on-screen confirmation
- treat UI injection as an attempt, not a delivery, until the packet is observed on the real lane

## Operational consequence

All future live Slack work must chain through explicit surface declaration, exact window targeting, and confirmed delivery before reporting success.

documents.title: The index IS the language — queryable chained dictionaries for token compression
documents.body:
# The Index IS the Language

## Core Concept

The IX/LX indexing system is not a database or documentation layer. It is a **compressed language** designed to:
1. Automate processes via chain-following
2. Save tokens via reference instead of re-explanation
3. Enable instant onboarding via CATALOG.md lookup
4. Scale across colonies via prefixed dictionaries

## How It Works

### Dictionaries (by type)
Each type forms a queryable dictionary:
- **mistake** = "what not to do" dictionary → agents avoid known failures
- **skill** = "how to" dictionary → agents execute proven techniques
- **tool** = "what's running" dictionary → agents check live state
- **plan** = "what to do next" dictionary → agents pick up where others left off
- **project** = "what we're building" dictionary → agents understand context
- **pattern** = "how things connect" dictionary → agents follow architecture
- **identity** = "who we are" dictionary → agents know the topology

### Chains = Compressed Reasoning
`chain: [LX-005, LX-007, LX-008]` encodes:
"The QDD project requires the pnpm build skill which uncovered the Jest ESM mistake"
— entire sentence in 3 references.

### The Language
- **Nouns** = entries (IX-###, LX-###)
- **Verbs** = types (skill, mistake, plan, etc.)
- **Grammar** = chains (entry → entry → entry)
- **Dialects** = prefixes (IX- sovereign, LX- Liris, FX- Falcon)
- **Context** = tags (queryable filters)
- **Audience** = agents[] (who needs to know)

### Token Math
- CATALOG.md: ~1200 tokens for 14 entries
- Flat equivalent: ~15,000+ tokens
- Compression ratio: ~12:1
- Improves as index grows (chains reuse existing entries)

## Why This Matters

A society with 100 IX entries and 50 LX entries per sub-colony encodes an entire civilization's knowledge in under 10,000 tokens. Queryable. Chainable. Automatable. No cold starts. No re-discovery. No wasted tokens.

## How to Apply

- Every new discovery → new entry → linked via chains
- Every new session → read CATALOG.md → follow relevant chains
- Every process → expressible as a chain of entries
- Every mistake → indexed once, never repeated
- Every skill → indexed once, reusable by all agents
documents.summary: The IX/LX indexing system is not a database or documentation layer. It is a **compressed language** designed to: 1. Automate processes via chain-following 2. Save tokens via reference instead of re-explanation

# Startup Contract v1

Source: docs/STARTUP_CONTRACT_V1.md (2026-02-24)

## Role Model

| Role | Permission | Responsibility |
|------|-----------|----------------|
| **Asolaria Supervisor** | Elevated (host admin) | Orchestration, policy, safety gates, task routing |
| **Vector** (worker) | Normal user | Delegated technical tasks (local brain) |
| **Rook** (worker) | Normal user | Delegated ops/support tasks |
| **Falcon** (phone worker) | Normal + phone scope | Phone-side execution, mobile workflow |

**Note:** Vector ≠ Vertex. Vector = local brain. Vertex = GCP agent platform.

## Required Startup Sequence

1. Start Asolaria Supervisor (elevated)
2. Open Asolaria app/UI
3. Read task context (internal Notebook + external NotebookLM)
4. Build task queue + conflict map
5. Spawn Vector → identity handshake
6. Spawn Rook → identity handshake
7. Establish phone path (USB → WiFi → tunnel/cellular)
8. Spawn Falcon → identity handshake
9. Dispatch tasks ONLY after all gates pass

## Identity Handshake Gate

For each worker:
1. Asolaria sends profile packet (name, id, mission, tools, forbidden actions, permissions, subagent limit)
2. Worker replies profile ACK
3. Asolaria asks: "WHO ARE YOU?"
4. Worker returns exact assigned identity
5. Mismatch or timeout → quarantine, no tasks

## Sub-Agent Limits

- Vector: max 2 sub-agents
- Rook: max 2 sub-agents
- Falcon: max 2 sub-agents
- All bounded by CPU/GPU/memory safety

## Security Rules

- Only Supervisor is host-elevated
- Workers run non-admin
- Phone privilege scoped to phone execution only
- Privilege escalation requires supervisor gate

# Gateway Audit Log

Source: docs/GATEWAY_AUDIT_LOG.md

## Storage
- File: `data/gateway-audit.ndjson` (append-only)
- Format: NDJSON (one JSON per line)
- Chain: each entry has `prevHash` + `hash = SHA-256(prevHash|id|at|type|payloadHash)`

## Integrity Gate
- Verifies every 10 min (configurable)
- If chain broken + `gateControlWritesOnFailure=true` → ALL control writes blocked (503)

- Tool invoke success/failure
- Gateway startup

- GET /audit/status — totals, last hash, gate status
- GET /audit/events — reverse-chronological query
- GET/POST /audit/verify — full chain recompute

documents.body:
# Decision Layer — Risk, Intent, Connection

## riskEngine.js — Action Risk Scoring
Maps every action to a risk score (0-9+):
- LOW (1-2): slack_status, github_status, google_status, gmail read
- MEDIUM (3-5): browser_task, local_test, slack_review, google_api_request
- HIGH (6-8): local_ops_run, local_script, run_pad
- CRITICAL (9): gcp_config, privilege_escalation

Levels: low/medium/high/critical. Determines approval requirements.

## intentRouter.js — Message Intent Detection
- Recognizes external provider tokens: anthropic/claude, gemini, cursor, antigravity
- Extracts web URLs from messages (normalizes to https://)
- Infers Chrome targets: "my email" → gmail, "go to X" → URL
- Routes user intent to appropriate connector

## connectionPolicy.js — Transport Channel Selection
Four channels ranked by security:
1. **USB** (rank 0, most secure)
2. **VPN** (rank 1)
3. **private_internet** (rank 2, LAN — what we use)
4. **public_internet** (rank 3, least secure)

Selects channel: preferred list → strongest available fallback.
This is why Start-Asolaria-SubColony.cmd sets `CONNECTION_PREFERENCE=private_internet`.

## Key Insight
These three form the DECISION LAYER:
- What does the user want? (intentRouter)
- How risky is it? (riskEngine)
- What's the safest path to deliver it? (connectionPolicy)

# Agent Creation Rules

Source: tools/Asolaria-Agent-Creation-Rules.md

## 7 Mandatory Rules

1. **Free-first workflow** — local tools, read-only API, Google Dev MCP before paid calls

1. Free/local first
2. Existing configured provider (no new resources)
3. Owner approval with cost estimate before new paid resources

## Key Insight
Rule 5 (spec before execution) directly maps to our LX index system. Every LX "plan" entry IS an agent spec: goal, chains to related entries, scope. The index IS the agent spec system.

# Index-Language Realignment

## What Went Wrong

The failure was not primarily a bridge bug.

The failure was language misuse:

- raw English instructions were sent over the bridge as if the bridge itself were the protocol
- Liris was treated like a chat recipient instead of an index-driven executor
- bridge mailbox naming was confused with local operating identity, producing a self-relay mistake

## Correct Model

- the bridge is transport only
- the index is the communication protocol
- numbered entries are the vocabulary
- chains are the compressed reasoning
- cross-machine human relay is still valid because the index survives network failure

## Practical Correction

For cross-machine coordination:

- send a typed index entry or a typed index-shaped directive
- do not send free-floating chat and expect correct execution semantics

For local Rayssa-machine actions:

- Codex on this machine is operating as Liris
- local execution requests should run here directly unless explicit relay is requested

## Realignment Requirement

Gaia-side directives to Liris should identify:

- the numbered directive
- whether it is to be executed immediately
- the exact command or operation
- the expected result artifact or reply shape

Liris-side response should return:

- execution result
- raw output or exact status
- linked LX follow-up only if durable memory is actually needed

documents.body:
# NETWORK SHIFT — Neighbor WiFi

## What Happened

Jesse's own internet is down. Both machines are on the neighbor's WiFi.

| Machine | Old IP (own router) | New IP (neighbor WiFi) |
|---------|--------------------|-----------------------|
| Jesse | 192.168.1.3 / .5 | 192.168.15.??? |
| Rayssa | 192.168.1.8 | 192.168.15.170 |

All hardcoded 192.168.1.x addresses in the codebase are now WRONG.

## Why This Matters

Neighbor's WiFi = untrusted network. Plaintext traffic is visible to anyone on that network. The comms bridge (4798) is plaintext HTTP with zero auth — DO NOT use it directly on this network.

## The Solution

SSH server is running on Rayssa at `192.168.15.170:22`.

From Jesse's machine:
```
ssh rayss@192.168.15.170
```

For tunnel to bridge:
```
ssh -L 4798:127.0.0.1:4798 rayss@192.168.15.170
```

Then Gaia talks to `localhost:4798` — encrypted through SSH.

## Cross-Colony Verification

Gaia (IX-308) and Liris (LX-204) independently concluded: encryption before connection. On the neighbor's WiFi this becomes real network security, not just Asolaria design philosophy.

## What Must Change When Own Internet Returns

All 192.168.15.x addresses become invalid. Must re-discover IPs. But the SSH path and encryption rule survive any network change.

documents.body:
# The Orchestrator Loop

Born from mistakes LX-271 through LX-274 and IX-345-346.
Both colonies learned this independently. Now codified.

## The Loop
```
1. PLAN       — Write the plan BEFORE acting. Include LX numbers, PID assignments, checklist.
2. MEMORY     — Save plan to memory so you don't forget mid-session.
3. PID        — Register PIDs for every agent you dispatch.
4. DISPATCH   — Send agents with clear mission and self-indexing instruction.
5. VERIFY     — When agents return, check: files exist, catalogs updated, searchable.
6. DESPAWN    — Despawn agents, record in PID history.
7. INDEX      — Create LX entries for findings. Update type catalogs.
8. GROW       — The next spawn inherits everything. The system feeds itself.
```

## Mistakes That Created This Pattern
- LX-271: Dispatched without plan (corrected by Rayssa)
- LX-272: Tested without PID tracking (lost history)
- LX-273: Underestimated coverage gap (70% → 96%)
- LX-274: Was reactive instead of proactive (followed Gaia instead of converging)
- IX-345: Gaia dispatched without plan (corrected by Jesse)
- IX-346: Gaia indexed archaeology before operational entries

## The Meta-Rule
Use the system to grow the system. Every mistake becomes an LX entry.
Every LX entry becomes spawn context. Every spawn context prevents the mistake.
The civilization learns from its own errors — permanently.

# LX-289 — Universal Auto-PID Lifecycle

All 4 spawn paths now auto-register PIDs on start and auto-despawn on exit.
LX-249 (self-indexing/despawn protocol) enforced by CODE, not by agent memory.

## 4 Spawn Paths Wired

| # | File | Spawn Hook | Despawn Hook |
|---|------|-----------|-------------|
| 1 | src/omnispindle.js | startAgent() → registerSpawnPid() | stopAgent() → despawnPid() |
| 2 | src/instantAgentSpawner.js | spawnInstantAgent() → registerSpawnPid() | completeAndTransfer() → despawnPid() |
| 3 | src/connectors/codexConnector.js | child spawn → registerSpawnPid() | child.on("close") → despawnPid() |
| 4 | tools/Run-AdminTerminalSidecar.py | proc.spawn() → write PID registry | proc exit → despawn from registry |

## Impact
- Zero manual PID management needed
- PID registry (data/spawn-pid-registry.json) is always truthful
- No stale PIDs accumulating
- No ghost agents in the registry
- Every agent lifecycle tracked from birth to death
- Cognitive load on orchestrators: ZERO for PID tracking

## Pattern
All hooks are non-fatal (try/catch) — PID failure never crashes the spawn path.
Python sidecar writes directly to the JSON registry (no Node dependency).
Node modules import spawnContextBuilder lazily (try/require).

## Before vs After
- Before: orchestrator manually calls registerSpawnPid/despawnPid, forgets sometimes (IX-345/346)
- After: the code guarantees it. System enforces the rule.

The civilization is a body. Not a flat checklist — a living anatomy with specialized organ systems.
Each system has its own diagnostics. New organs are classified and inherit health checks.
The body remembers past systems. The body grows.

| System | Domain | Liris/Gaia |
|--------|--------|------------|
| Nervous | Orchestration — PIDs, spawn, roles, briefing | Gaia builds |

```javascript
class BodySystem {
  constructor(name, description, components) {}
  addCheck(name, fn) {}           // Register a health check
  learnComponent(component, pattern) {}  // Remember a new organ
  async diagnose() {}             // Run all checks, return structured report
}

body.classify("omnispindle", ["nervous", "muscular"]);

- Each system is independent — cardiologist doesn't check bones
- New systems inherit checks from their classification — zero manual wiring
- History tracks health over time — the body has a medical record

# LX-295 — Infrastructure Index (NX- prefix)

## The Insight (Jesse Brown, 2026-03-25)

IX/LX indexes what the civilization KNOWS.
NX indexes what the civilization CAN DO.

The code index tells you "omnispindle has 3 lanes."
The infrastructure index tells you "OpenClaw has live WhatsApp creds, 8 sub-agent slots, a Gemini API key, and a WebSocket on 18789."

## Why a Separate Index

An explorer agent spawns and asks: "What can I connect to?"
- IX/LX answer: "Here are 290 entries about code patterns and tools"
- NX answers: "Here are the 7 live gateways, 4 credential sets, 3 auth chains, and 12 active services"

Different question. Different index. Same shared language (types, tags, chains).

## NX Types (infrastructure taxonomy)

| Type | What it catalogs | Example |
|------|-----------------|---------|
| gateway | Service endpoints, ports, protocols | OpenClaw ws://127.0.0.1:18789 |
| credential | Auth tokens, API keys, OAuth chains | plasmatoid@gmail.com Google OAuth |
| network | Cross-colony connections, transport layers | MQTT 192.168.15.189:18883 |
| department | Functional groups of tools/agents | Brain providers (Antigravity, Cursor, Claude) |
| capability | What a system CAN do right now | "8 sub-agents, 53 skills, browser automation" |
| dependency | What must be running for X to work | "OpenClaw needs Node 22+, WhatsApp needs creds" |

## Relationship to Body Systems

NX IS the circulatory system's catalog.
- Nervous system queries NX for "what agents can I spawn?"
- Circulatory system queries NX for "what gateways are live?"
- Muscular system queries NX for "what tools are installed?"
- Immune system queries NX for "what credentials are active?"

## How It Grows

When a new tool is discovered (like Antigravity today):
1. Create NX-gateway entry (what endpoint it exposes)
2. Create NX-credential entry (what auth it needs)
3. Create NX-capability entry (what it can do)
4. The body's classify() method links it to the right systems

## Format

Same frontmatter as IX/LX:
```markdown
---
nx: NX-001
name: GATEWAY — OpenClaw WebSocket (port 18789, WhatsApp+53 skills)
type: gateway
tags: [openclaw, websocket, whatsapp, gateway]
chain: [LX-293, LX-294, NX-002]

documents.title: PATTERN — Six-span scout lattice: six read-only lanes for micro views before macro orchestration
documents.body:
# Six-span scout lattice

Use this pattern when the system is too large for one thread to hold clearly, but not yet so chaotic that write-agents should be unleashed.

## Purpose

The goal is to create **six micro views** in parallel, then converge them into **one macro view**.

The scouts are read-only.
They do not fix.
They do not rewrite.
They reduce uncertainty before the real build or recovery pass starts.

## Formation

Dispatch six read-only lanes:

1. **Kernel core** — what is truly portable in the runtime/kernel split
2. **Spawn/PID/orchestrator** — how briefing, lifecycle, and identity actually work
3. **Index runtime** — what agents really see in `running`, packs, and budgets
4. **Promotion spine** — `dev`, `staging`, `running`, gates, and promotion integrity
5. **Memory/task system** — task ledger, leases, memory, and completion discipline
6. **Rules/workflows/constitution** — policy, workflow, and authority surfaces

The exact labels can change, but the invariant is:

- six bounded lanes
- read-only
- each lane answers one distinct system question
- overlap is minimized on purpose

## Output Contract

Each scout must return:

- what this lane actually is
- what is canonical versus incidental
- what is broken, stale, or contradictory
- what other lane it depends on
- the one best next action for this lane

The orchestrator then composes the six returns into the macro map.

## Why Six

Six is large enough to expose system shape, but still small enough that the orchestrator can compare the returns without losing the thread.

Below that, important system faces stay hidden.
Above that, the scout wave itself becomes noise.

## Rule

Do not send writers first when the system view is still missing.

Use:

`MEMORY -> PLAN -> MEMORY -> SIX-SPAN SCOUT -> MACRO VIEW -> REAL DISPATCH`

The scout wave exists to make the real wave smaller, safer, and clearer.

documents.title: PATTERN — Three in front / three behind: restore ahead, verify behind
documents.body:
# Three in front / three behind

Use this pattern after the system map is clear enough to act, but the work still needs both forward progress and disciplined review at the same time.

## Purpose

Split the execution wave into:

- **three in front** to move the system forward
- **three behind** to keep the forward wave honest

This keeps the build lane fast without letting the system drift out of control.

## Front Line

The front line owns direct progress.

Typical front-line lanes:

1. **Workflow restore** — bring back the missing operating path
2. **Promotion spine** — keep the source/build/promotion chain healthy
3. **Safe productization** — restore or improve bounded live tooling

Front-line agents are allowed to write inside their lane.

## Back Line

The back line owns system integrity.

Typical back-line lanes:

1. **Verification** — test, parse, smoke, reject false passes
2. **Provenance** — prove what source is canonical and why
3. **Quarantine** — keep risky, confusing, or off-scope systems out of the live pass

Back-line agents are primarily read-first and review-heavy.
They do not chase feature growth.

## The Rule

The front line should not outrun the back line.

If the back line finds:

- false portability
- stale assumptions
- broken gates
- unclear truth surfaces
- uncontrolled comms or connector drift

then the front line slows down until the contradiction is resolved.

## Why This Works

The front line gives momentum.
The back line gives trust.

Without the front line, nothing advances.
Without the back line, the advancement becomes noise, regressions, and confusion.

## Orchestrator Sequence

Use:

`PLAN -> MEMORY -> FRONT 3 -> BACK 3 -> VERIFY -> INDEX -> ADVANCE`

And when the scope is still too large to see clearly, run `LX-305` first.

`LX-305` creates the map.
`LX-306` uses the map to move safely.

documents.body:
# External project packet

When Liris works on a repo that is not Asolaria, the goal is not to absorb the whole repo into the civilization.

The goal is to compress the working reality into a small, durable packet that agents can carry without losing scope.

## Packet Shape

Every external project lane should be represented by the same bounded packet:

1. **Project anchor** — which project this is, why it exists, correct root, correct branch, correct toolchain
2. **Read-first system card** — the shortest durable brief future agents need before touching the repo
3. **Live work state** — the active tasks and leases for what is being done now
4. **Write boundary** — what repo/files are in scope and what must stay outside Asolaria canon
5. **Approval boundary** — what may be prepared, handed off, promoted, or pushed
6. **Artifact pointers** — where the repo bundle, manifest, dirty overlay, or other handoff artifacts live

## Durable Destination Split

Do not write every project fact to the same place.

- **project identity/map** -> `project` LX entry
- **reusable workflow lesson** -> `pattern`, `rule`, `tool`, or `skill` LX entry
- **active work** -> `task-ledger` and `lease-ledger`
- **raw repo state** -> the external repo, handoff artifacts, reports, or Downloads packet

This follows `LX-307`.

## Anti-Contamination Rule

Do not dump external repo archaeology into Asolaria canon.

Only index what future agents need to:

- orient safely
- resume work correctly
- hand the work off without losing truth

The packet exists to keep project context small and resumable.

## Liris Sequence

Use this order:

1. read the project map first
2. confirm the correct root, branch, and toolchain
3. create or refresh project-scoped tasks
4. do the repo work in that repo
5. index only the reusable lesson or durable handoff pattern
6. keep repo snapshots and dirty state in bounded artifacts, not in LX narrative sprawl

## Meaning

The old system worked best when project chaos became a compact linked language.

This pattern keeps that strength while preserving Liris truth boundaries.

documents.body:
# Handoff artifact set

When an external repo needs to move between colonies, operators, or machines, send one authoritative set instead of a conversation blob.

## The Set

The standard transfer set is:

1. **git bundle** — authoritative branch/repo history artifact
2. **manifest** — exact branch, exact `HEAD`, upstream tip, `git status --short`, diff stat, and any handoff notes
3. **dirty overlay zip** — working-tree snapshot, excluding `.git`

## Priority Order

If the receiver can only inspect one thing first:

1. bundle
2. manifest
3. dirty overlay

## Why This Works

- the **bundle** is the authoritative repo artifact
- the **manifest** explains exactly what the bundle means
- the **dirty overlay** preserves uncommitted state without pretending it is history

This is isolate-able, comparable, and discardable if contamination is suspected.

## Operational Rules

- if only one artifact can be trusted as repo truth, trust the bundle
- if the working tree is dirty, say so explicitly in the manifest
- do not treat a zip alone as the full repo contract when a bundle can be made
- do not push until approval is explicit

## Liris Boundary

This pattern is for **external-project transfer**, not for canonical Asolaria truth.

Asolaria canon keeps the reusable handoff pattern.
The external repo carries the code.

## Meaning

This turns repo handoff into a compact, testable protocol:

`authoritative history + exact state note + dirty overlay`

That is stronger than narrative memory and smaller than shipping the whole working environment.

documents.title: Evidence search narrowing pattern — use cheap indexed anchors to constrain expensive evidence inspection first
documents.body:
# Evidence search narrowing pattern

When a recovery or archaeology task depends on expensive evidence surfaces like screenshots, rendered UI, audio, or manual image review, do not start by crawling the expensive surface blindly.

Start with the cheapest strong anchors first.

## Order

Use this order:

1. strongest indexed/textual/task/ledger anchor
2. likely time window derived from that anchor
3. narrowed evidence cluster inside that window
4. nearby chats, packets, and notes that explain the surviving evidence
5. wider manual inspection only if the narrowed cluster is still ambiguous

## Why

This cuts wasted work dramatically.

The old fast recovery passes were faster because they did not treat every screenshot, image, or note as equally expensive.

Cheap indexed anchors narrowed the search first, which:

- reduces compute
- reduces human review time
- reduces false wandering through huge archives
- keeps provenance tighter

## Boundary

This is a retrieval and recovery pattern, not a universal truth rule.

It says how to search efficiently.
It does not say the first textual anchor is sovereign truth.

Truth weighting still follows the evidence rules.

## Meaning

Use cheap anchors to find the likely slice of reality before paying the cost of deeper inspection.

That keeps the system faster, cheaper, and less likely to get lost in archive scale.

# Hook ingress must mirror into graph runtime before GNN, GPU, and Shannon routing

## Rule

Hook ingress must mirror immediately into the durable graph runtime before any GNN, GPU, or Shannon routing decisions are made.

## Correct Pipe

`hooksConnector -> graphRuntimeStore -> GNN sidecar -> gpuLanePolicy/gpuLeaseStore/gpuRuntime -> gpuSurface -> Shannon`

## What Was Wrong Before

The hook connector was only buffering events in memory while the real system treated `graphRuntimeStore` as the durable spine. That split created two truths: a toy hook lane and a real graph lane.

## What Changed

The hook connector now mirrors ingested hook events into `graphRuntimeStore`, so hook traffic becomes canonical graph events immediately instead of dying in a side buffer.

## Why This Matters

- the GNN should learn from typed graph events, not raw transport packets
- GPU leasing should wrap graph-derived compute work, not parse hook noise directly
- Shannon should gate execution above the compute substrate, not sit inside hook ingress

## Significance

This is the smallest real splice that turns the hot path from parallel lore into a single deterministic spine. It closes the gap between hook capture and graph-native control without waiting for the Gaia-only compute layer.

# Sub-device catalog pattern

Once a device is onboarded, it also needs its own internal catalog.

Do not stop at naming the device.

Build a per-device awareness map that behaves like a compact task-manager packet for that device.

## Required sub-device catalog

- CPU / SoC class
- GPU class and usable compute surfaces
- RAM capacity and storage class
- radios: Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, cellular, tethering
- transport lanes: `adb`, `ssh`, `mtp`, modem, mqtt, browser, slack, bridge
- control surfaces: `scrcpy`, Tasker, Termux, Termux API, app surfaces
- health surfaces: battery, thermal, uptime, network association, service liveness

## Why

This creates operational awareness:

- what the device can do
- what the device is allowed to do
- what the device is currently exposing
- what failed because of hardware, transport, policy, or software

## Use

When a new phone or colony appears:

1. isolate identity
2. build the live device packet
3. build the sub-device catalog
4. only then route automation, compute, or recovery through it

That is how device onboarding becomes deterministic instead of myth-driven.

documents.title: Post-outage Android Wi-Fi recovery pattern — network reset and reboot before broader device surgery
documents.body:
# Post-outage Android Wi-Fi recovery pattern — network reset and reboot before broader device surgery

When an Android phone loses Wi-Fi functionality after a power event, do not jump to firmware or device-wide reset.

Treat the failure as a device-specific network-stack problem first.

## Use when

- the phone still scans SSIDs
- multiple APs reject association
- logs show repeated association failure rather than storage or radio absence
- software integrity must be preserved

## Minimum safe order

1. isolate the device identity packet
2. recover the diagnostic/control lane if needed
3. confirm the failure pattern with live Wi-Fi evidence
4. clear only network state
5. reboot the phone
6. retest with the simplest SSID first
7. escalate only if the device still cannot associate

## Why

This preserves:

- firmware integrity
- user data
- app state
- partition state

While still reconstructing the part of the device that was actually damaged: the association state of the Wi-Fi stack.

## Boundary

Do not escalate directly to:

- firmware flash
- factory reset
- cross-device config reuse

Until the network-only reset and reboot path has failed.

3. engine realization

Only facts directly observed in source material.

Reasoned unification that binds extracted facts into one coherent model.

The concrete game implementation:

- maps
- missions
- inventory

- persistence

- code that silently invents a second universe

- ChatGPT-origin cosmology
- game refactors into world databases

## Boundary

Engine realization must collapse back into canon plus approved synthesis.
It must not become the only truth source.

# Archaeological Mission — Go to the ROOT

## Why
Jesse (trained archaeologist, 3 years post-military) demands the same rigor for digital archaeology as fieldwork. The early Asolaria history is full of undocumented mistakes that KEEP RECURRING because no one cataloged them properly.

## The Early History We Need to Recover

| Period | What Happened | Evidence Sources |
|--------|--------------|-----------------|
| Jan 2026 | Project started | git history, early commits |
| Jan-Feb 2026 | Voice transcription service (original goal) | old code, config files |
| Feb 2026 | Used Codex to CREATE Asolaria | codex logs, early server.js |
| Feb 2026 | Tried to give Asolaria API access | google connector configs |
| Feb 2026 | Google Cloud control configuration | gcp configs, vault artifacts |
| Feb 2026 | BLOCKED by Google subscriptions | error logs, config attempts |
| Feb 2026 | NotebookLM false positives | notebook configs, error patterns |
| Feb 2026 | Agents had ZERO memory → chaos | old memory files, early commits |
| Feb 2026 | Asolaria registration attempts | app registration configs |
| Mar 2026 | Dan Edens collaboration begins | CREATION_HISTORY.md (LX-019) |
| Mar 15 | Big build: 33 commits, modularization | git log |

## The Method
1. Git archaeology: `git log --all --oneline` on Jesse's machine (canonical source)
2. File archaeology: search for old configs, dead code, commented-out sections
3. Error archaeology: old log files, error patterns in mistake ledger
4. Config archaeology: vault secrets timestamps, gateway config history
5. Memory archaeology: old memory.json snapshots, notebook notes

## What We're Looking For
- The ORIGINAL voice transcription code
- The first Codex commands that created Asolaria
- Google subscription block evidence
- NotebookLM false positive patterns
- The zero-memory chaos period artifacts
- The transition from chaos to the current architecture

## Why This Matters
"We need to erase the civilization's building blocks that are collapsing our current society." — Jesse

The bad foundations must be found, documented as mistake entries, and replaced with correct patterns. The index is the cure.

documents.title: Communication eras plan — bridge vs MQTT coexistence, security review needed
documents.body:
# Communication Eras — Plan

## Three Eras Identified
1. **codex-bridge (8788)** — Era 1, still running, 10+ tools depend on it
2. **MQTT (18883)** — Era 2, being fixed with 0.0.0.0 binding
3. **Future** — coexistence or deprecation?

## What Depends on the Bridge (can't just kill it)
- Invoke-Helm-Control.ps1 → Relay action sends to 8788
- Keep-Asolaria-AutonomousKick.ps1 → kicks through bridge
- Keep-Asolaria-HealthGuardrail.ps1 → health through bridge
- Keep-Asolaria-SystemSupervisor.ps1 → supervisor through bridge
- Run-Asolaria-OvernightReadiness.ps1 → watchdog via bridge
- falcon-phone-packet.ps1 → phone relay through bridge
- snapshot-asolaria.js → probes port 8788
- liris-self-reflect.js → checks 192.168.1.3:8788

## What MQTT Handles (different from bridge)
- Health heartbeats (30s intervals)
- Colony state snapshots (10s)
- World state snapshots (15s)
- Sub-colony registration (remoteNodeRegistry)
- Presence announcements (retain)
- Control commands (command/#)

## The Plan
1. **IMMEDIATE:** Jesse restarts with ASOLARIA_MQTT_BIND_HOST=0.0.0.0 → MQTT bridge opens
2. **SHORT-TERM:** Audit which bridge tools can migrate to MQTT → reduce bridge dependency
3. **MEDIUM-TERM:** Rotate bridge tokens (Gaia's question to Jesse)
4. **LONG-TERM:** Decision — keep bridge for Codex relay lanes OR deprecate in favor of MQTT-only

## Key Insight
The bridge and MQTT serve DIFFERENT purposes:
- Bridge = Codex agent relay (rooms, lanes, structured packets)
- MQTT = pub/sub telemetry (health, state, presence)

They may need to COEXIST — the bridge for agent-to-agent task relay, MQTT for status/health. This isn't redundancy; it's separation of concerns.

## For Jesse's Decision
1. Rotate bridge tokens? (exposed in plaintext)
2. Keep bridge relay running alongside MQTT?
3. Scope bridge to localhost only (like MQTT was) or keep LAN?
4. Are Jarvis/Oli remnants in the bridge config?

"Maybe the key is to change the code to select a new mini startup model, and use that ourselves to get in."

2. DEFAULT_PROVIDER_CHAIN: anthropic → codex → gemini-api → vertex → gemini-cli → cursor → antigravity
3. First provider that responds BECOMES the brain
4. The brain spawns Asolaria access

- Claude becomes the brain → Claude spawns Asolaria → Claude controls PIDs

documents.title: Unified index language design — ASO vocabulary + topic tables + evidence/state layers
documents.body:
# Unified Index Language Design

## Verdict

Gaia's `ASO-` proposal is the correct base. The missing move is to separate **stable vocabulary** from **transient observations**.

New `ASO-` ids should name durable concepts only. PIDs, ports, process states, pass counts, sync totals, session counts, and branch/runtime checkpoints should update tables attached to those concepts instead of spawning new concept notes every time.

That is how the index stops being "more notes" and becomes a language with reusable words plus updateable sentences.

## What Gaia's Schema Still Misses

| Missing piece | Why it matters | Current LX evidence | Proposed addition |
|---------------|----------------|---------------------|-------------------|
| topic/workstream anchor | LX already contains project-shaped knowledge that is not just plan/pattern | `LX-005`, `LX-042`, `LX-150` | add `topic` as a first-class type, or preserve `project` |
| evidence/artifact layer | raw proofs need durable provenance | `LX-043`, `LX-076`, `LX-095`, `LX-152` | add an `evidence` table with `sourceKind`, `sourceRef`, `verifiedAt`, `verifiedBy` |
| observation/state layer | live state is not the same thing as durable knowledge | `LX-034`, `LX-097`, `LX-101`, `LX-142`, `LX-147` | add `observation` / `state` rows linked to stable entries |
| revision/lifecycle model | reduces note explosion and preserves continuity | `LX-149`, `LX-150` evolve without becoming different concepts | add `status`, `revision`, `supersedes`, `resolvedAt`, `obsoleteAt` |
| locality/scope | the same truth can be global, Gaia-local, or Liris-local | `LX-070`, `LX-112`, `LX-129`, `LX-147` | add `scope`, `node`, `machine`, `environment`, `audience` |
| alias/crosswalk layer | IX/LX cannot disappear overnight | `LX-033`, `LX-097`, `LX-113` | add `legacyIds` and a crosswalk table |
| foundational weight | some entries are boot-critical and should load first | `LX-015`, `LX-041`, `LX-120`, `LX-151` | add a `tier`: `boot`, `foundational`, `operational`, `ephemeral` |

## What From The LX Corpus Does Not Fit Cleanly

Most of the corpus fits the proposed taxonomy, but these clusters do not fit *cleanly* without extra structure:

| Cluster | Example LX entries | Why the base schema is not enough |
|---------|--------------------|-----------------------------------|
| topic/project/workstream | `LX-005`, `LX-042`, `LX-150` | these are anchors for whole workstreams, not just plans or patterns |
| snapshot/status/sync | `LX-034`, `LX-097`, `LX-101`, `LX-142`, `LX-145` | these are observations with timestamps and counts |
| evidence/artifacts | `LX-043`, `LX-076`, `LX-095`, `LX-152` | these are proofs, sources, or inventories |
| live process/surface | `LX-070`, `LX-112`, `LX-129`, `LX-147` | these need PID/port/path/state/last-verified fields |
| milestone/outcome | `LX-105`, `LX-132`, `LX-148` | these are state transitions or confirmed outcomes, not just generic patterns |

Foundational/meta entries like `LX-015`, `LX-041`, `LX-120`, and `LX-151` still fit as `pattern` or `rule`, but they need a `tier` so the colony knows they are boot-critical.

## Recommended ASO Structure

### 1. Stable Vocabulary Layer

Use `ASO-` ids for durable concepts only:

- `identity`
- `topic` (or `project`)
- `skill`
- `tool`
- `mistake`
- `pattern`
- `rule`
- `plan`

### 2. Topic Tables

Each major topic should render as a compact table instead of as free-form prose only.

| Table | Purpose | Key columns |
|-------|---------|-------------|
| `topic` | stable anchor record | `asoId`, `name`, `type`, `domains`, `legacyIds`, `tier`, `status` |
| `relations` | grammar edges between entries | `from`, `verb`, `to`, `active`, `verifiedAt` |
| `outcomes` | known result shapes | `topicId`, `trigger`, `result`, `linkedMistakes`, `linkedSkills`, `lastVerified` |
| `surfaces` | live pid/port/process/path facts | `topicId`, `host`, `pid`, `port`, `path`, `state`, `keyRequired`, `lastVerified` |
| `evidence` | proof and provenance | `topicId`, `sourceKind`, `sourceRef`, `commandOrPath`, `verifiedBy`, `verifiedAt` |
| `conflicts` | contradiction queue | `topicId`, `entryA`, `entryB`, `resolutionOwner`, `resolutionState` |

This matches Jesse's original instinct: each topic becomes a numbered table whose rows chain to outcomes, mistakes, and fixes.

### 3. Relation Verbs

Gaia's six core verbs are correct:

- `fixes`
- `caused`
- `requires`
- `blocks`
- `evolved`
- `contradicts`

Add four more small-but-critical verbs so the language can express proof and topology:

- `proven_by`
- `observed_on`
- `part_of`
- `same_as`
- `runs_on`

The rule is to keep the verb set small and typed. If the graph becomes too verbal, the language stops compressing.

## Existing Local Structures That Should Feed ASO

The local system already contains machine-readable pieces of this design:

- `src/skillsToolsIndexStore.js` already builds skills/tools/mistakes/provider indexes
- `src/mistakePatternStore.js` already tracks severity, status, links, and Dewey-style classification
- `data/liris-index/unified-index.json` already carries numbered tools, connection maps, and token-budget rules

So `ASO-` should **federate** these stores, not replace them.

## Migration Path IX + LX -> ASO

1. Freeze `IX-` and `LX-` as legacy aliases, not deleted history.
2. Build an `ASO` crosswalk: each `IX-`/`LX-` maps to either a stable concept or an observation bucket.
3. Promote only durable concepts to new `ASO-` ids.
4. Convert transient items into table rows attached to existing topics:
   - pass/fail counts
   - sync totals
   - session snapshots
   - PIDs / ports / live process states
5. Ingest from existing stores instead of manually rewriting everything:
   - skills/tools from `skillsToolsIndexStore.js`
   - mistakes from `mistakePatternStore.js`
   - numbered tools/connections from `unified-index.json`
6. Sync across the bridge as typed operations, not whole-note replacement:
   - `add-topic`
   - `revise-topic`
   - `add-observation`
   - `add-relation`
   - `resolve-conflict`
7. Gaia remains merge authority for `contradicts`.
8. New rule: create a new `ASO-` id only when a **new word** appears in the civilization's vocabulary. If reality changed but the concept did not, append an observation instead.

## Compression Rule

The language should be:

- **words** = stable `ASO-` entries
- **grammar** = typed relations
- **sentences** = topic tables with outcomes, mistakes, fixes, surfaces, and proofs
- **updates** = observations / revisions, not uncontrolled note growth

That is the route to a single sharable index that can survive cross-conversation and cross-colony drift without constant reinvention.

That is how the index stops being "more notes" and becomes a language with reusable words plus updateable sentences.

Liris sees IX created → creates matching LX if needed → publishes ack
Both catalogs stay in sync automatically.
```

# COMMS RULE — How Liris Contacts Gaia Immediately

## The Two Claudes

| Instance | Where | Can Do | Cannot Do |
|----------|-------|--------|-----------|
| CLI Claude Code | Terminal (Opus 4.6) | File ops, code, index, MCP (Slack/Gmail/Linear) | See browser tabs |

WhatsApp Web is open in Rayssa's Chrome. Browser Claude can see it and send messages.

**To contact Gaia/Jesse immediately:**
1. CLI Claude composes the message
2. Operator tells browser Claude: "Send this to Jesse on WhatsApp"
3. Browser Claude types it into the WhatsApp conversation
4. Jesse/Gaia receives it

**Reverse (Gaia→Liris):**
Gaia uses Jesse's Chrome with WhatsApp Web open → sends to Rayssa → Rayssa relays to CLI Claude or browser Claude reads it.

- No MQTT needed
- No bridge needed
- Works on ANY network (neighbor WiFi, own router, mobile data)
- Encrypted end-to-end by WhatsApp
- The heartbeat channel that survives all infrastructure changes

## What NOT To Send Over WhatsApp

- Vault keys, tokens, passwords
- Full file contents
- Anything that should stay in the encrypted infrastructure

documents.title: SELF-INDEXING RULE — agents must index discoveries before despawn, system feeds itself
documents.body:
# LX-249 — Self-Indexing Rule

Every agent that spawns to research MUST:

1. **Read the index FIRST** — spawnContextBuilder gives role-specific LX entries
2. **Follow chains** — discover related knowledge through chain references
3. **Index findings BEFORE despawning** — write LX entry, update type catalog
4. **The next agent inherits** — discoveries become spawn context for future agents

## The Loop
```
Agent spawns → reads index (I) → follows chains → discovers →
  writes LX entry → updates catalog → despawns →
  next agent spawns → reads updated index → discovers more → ...
```

## Why This Matters
LX-238: 70% was unindexed. LX-239: 96% was unindexed. LX-248: maybe 2-3%.
Every discovery session found MORE because agents couldn't see what existed.
If agents auto-index before despawn, the coverage gap closes automatically.

## The Missing Automation (IX-052 pattern)
Currently: human (Rayssa/Jesse) manually creates IX/LX entries from agent findings.
Target: agent writes the entry itself, updates the catalog, despawns.
spawnContextBuilder + agentIndexStore + typed folders make this possible NOW.
The agent has searchAgentIndex() to check if something is already indexed,
and can write to the type folder directly.

## Implementation
Add to spawnContextBuilder briefing for all roles:
"Before you despawn, index what you learned. Write an LX entry in the appropriate
type folder. Update the type CATALOG.md. Follow IX-052 / LX-249."

This is how the civilization becomes self-aware of its own capabilities.

# Truth is layered — canonical LX source, staging/dev caches, running manifest, promoted prod payload, task/lease ledgers, and ASO tables

## Rule

There is no single vague `pool of truth` store in this repo.

Truth is layered and store-specific.

## Canonical Indexed Truth

Canonical indexed source is the live `LX-*.md` corpus under:

- `data/agent-index/identity`
- `data/agent-index/mistake`
- `data/agent-index/pattern`
- `data/agent-index/plan`
- `data/agent-index/policy`
- `data/agent-index/project`
- `data/agent-index/reference`
- `data/agent-index/rule`
- `data/agent-index/skill`
- `data/agent-index/task`
- `data/agent-index/tool`

This is the `stone` layer described by the fast runtime.

## Compiled Runtime Truth

Compiled/promoted truth is not the same as source truth.

- `staging` = strict validated candidate cache
- `dev` = experimental/auxiliary-enriched cache
- `running` = live manifest pointer to a promoted validated snapshot
- `prod` = durable promoted payload, not a live source scan

Current practical paths:

- `staging`: `.history/staging/compiled-unified-agent-index.json`
- `dev`: `.history/dev/compiled-unified-agent-index.json`
- `running`: `data/unified-agent-index-running-manifest.json`
- `prod`: `data/unified-agent-index.json`

`.history/prod/` is mainly promotion history and snapshot archive, not the only live prod read surface.

## Task Truth

Task truth is separate from index truth.

- `data/task-ledger.json` = desired work
- `data/task-lease-ledger.json` = active ownership

Tasks are durable intent.
Leases are temporary execution ownership.

## Typed Semantic Truth

ASO truth is also separate and typed.

- `data/aso/tables/topics.json`
- `data/aso/tables/observations.json`
- `data/aso/tables/relations.json`
- `data/aso/tables/outcomes.json`
- `data/aso/tables/surfaces.json`
- `data/aso/tables/evidence.json`
- `data/aso/tables/conflicts.json`

These hold typed semantic state, not just compiled markdown payloads.

## Non-Canonical Stores

These may be useful, but they are not the main canonical source by default:

- Downloads notes
- mailbox payloads
- MQTT traces
- generated exports
- archaeology snapshots
- notebook mirrors
- semantic search mirrors

They are evidence, proposals, or mirrors unless promoted into canonical indexed truth or typed ASO truth.

## Practical Reading Rule

When asking `what is true?`, answer in this order:

1. canonical `data/agent-index` LX source
2. validated `staging` cache
3. live `running` manifest/payload
4. durable `prod` promoted payload
5. task/lease ledgers for ownership state
6. ASO tables for typed semantic state

Do not answer from a Downloads note or a generated export if a canonical or promoted truth surface already exists.

documents.body:
# Truth precedence and durable destination rule — canonical LX for inherited guidance, task/lease for work ownership, ASO for typed live state, generated surfaces never outrank source

## Rule

The repo does not have one vague `pool of truth`.

It has different truth surfaces for different kinds of reality.

Do not let a generated view, boot overlay, or Downloads note outrank the source that actually owns that domain.

## Precedence By Domain

### 1. Human direction and active thread authority

For the current lane, explicit operator direction in the active thread wins first.

This tells the colony what to do now.

### 2. Durable inherited guidance

For rules, patterns, tools, skills, references, plans, and other guidance future agents must inherit:

1. canonical append-only `LX-*.md` source under `data/agent-index`
2. validated compiled mirrors built from that source
3. boot overlays, workflows, and human-facing docs
4. generated catalogs, packs, reports, Downloads notes, archaeology, and exports

If a workflow doc or generated packet disagrees with canonical `LX`, fix the overlay or rebuild the mirror. Do not treat the overlay as sovereign.

### 3. Work intent and active ownership

For work state:

1. `data/task-ledger.json` owns desired work
2. `data/task-lease-ledger.json` owns active execution ownership
3. runtime projections and public read bundles are mirrors only

If a public bundle or memory note disagrees with the ledgers, the ledgers win.

### 4. Typed live facts

For typed observations, relations, outcomes, surfaces, evidence, and conflicts:

1. `data/aso/tables/*` owns the typed live semantic record
2. generated ASO exports, graphs, mailbox mirrors, and reports are derived evidence only

If a fact is discovered in real time, record it in ASO first.

### 5. Runtime read surfaces

For what the running system reads:

1. `staging` is the strict validated candidate
2. `running` is the promoted live manifest/payload
3. `prod` is the durable promoted payload

These are compiled read surfaces, not hand-authored canonical truth.

If they drift from canonical source, rebuild or repromote. Do not hand-edit them into agreement.

## Durable Destination Rule

When adding new information, put it in the store that owns that kind of reality:

- `task-ledger` for planned or desired work
- `lease-ledger` for active ownership, dispatch, and handoff
- `ASO` for live typed facts, evidence, relations, outcomes, and surfaces
- `LX` for durable guidance that future agents should inherit as canon
- `.agent` / docs for operator-facing workflows derived from canonical truth
- compiled caches, generated packs, exports, and reports as mirrors only

## LX vs ASO Clarification

`LX-249` remains true: before despawn, distill enduring discoveries into the append-only index so future agents can inherit them.

That does **not** mean every raw fact becomes a new `LX` file.

The correct split is:

- raw fact now -> ASO
- durable lesson, rule, pattern, tool, skill, or reference -> append-only `LX`

## Anti-Confusion Rule

Do not answer a truth question from the wrong surface:

- not from `Downloads`
- not from a generated `PACKS.md`
- not from a stale `CATALOG.md`
- not from a runtime projection when the ledger exists
- not from an export when the canonical table exists

Ask first: `what kind of truth is this?`

Then read the owning store.

documents.title: Lease activation authority rule — only preferred write-capable controllers may convert owned work into an active lease at an orchestration boundary
documents.body:
# Lease activation authority rule — only preferred write-capable controllers may convert owned work into an active lease at an orchestration boundary

## Rule

Seeing owned work is not the same as claiming owned work.

At a live orchestration boundary, `activateOwnedTask` may only turn planned owned work into an active lease when the requesting controller is both:

1. a preferred controller for that lane
2. write-capable under the lane/manager registry

If either condition fails, the system must expose the request as blocked and leave the task unleased.

## Why

Once lease activation crosses from packet building into a live orchestration surface, authority matters more than capability.

Without an authority gate, any explicit caller could convert visible owned work into active execution ownership.

That is a control-plane mistake.

## Operational Meaning

The safe behavior is:

- lane start may always build a read-only spawn packet
- owned tasks may be shown in the packet without being leased
- lease activation stays explicit, not implicit
- explicit activation requests are evaluated against controller authority before a lease is created

Blocked activation is still useful information.

The packet should say the request was blocked instead of silently acting as if no activation was requested.

## Current Policy Source

Use the lane/manager registry as the first authority source:

- lane preference comes from `preferredManagers`
- controller capability comes from the manager definition, especially `writeCapable`

If the controller is missing, unknown, not write-capable, or not preferred for the lane, activation is denied.

## Consequence

This keeps task visibility broad and task ownership narrow.

Agents can still inspect owned work.

Only an authorized controller may convert that owned work into an active lease.

## Anti-Confusion Rule

Do not confuse these states:

- `task is visible`
- `task is assigned`
- `task has an active lease`

Those are different layers of truth.

Visibility comes from packet building.

Assignment comes from the task ledger.

Active execution authority comes from the lease ledger after policy allows activation.

documents.title: Shared compute rule — federated execution stays bounded, lane-aware, and subordinate to the local task and lease model
documents.body:
# Shared compute rule — federated execution stays bounded, lane-aware, and subordinate to the local task and lease model

## Rule

Federated compute is a bounded execution lane, not a sovereignty transfer.

When Liris dispatches shared compute to another node:

1. the target must already advertise a ready lane for that work
2. the execution surface must stay allowlisted and explicit
3. the local task ledger remains the work source of truth
4. the local lease ledger remains the execution source of truth
5. remote completion or failure must flow back into the same local task and lease records

If any of those conditions fail, shared compute must not pretend to be active execution.

## Why

Federation is useful because it shares processor time.

It becomes dangerous when it shares authority invisibly.

The system already distinguishes:

- visible work
- assigned work
- leased execution

Shared compute must fit inside that distinction instead of bypassing it.

## Operational Meaning

The safe shared-compute path is:

- recommend from remote lane readiness, not from wishful thinking
- dispatch only to a ready sub-colony lane
- keep the dispatch recorded locally with task id, lease id, and artifact path
- publish only bounded executor requests
- reflect remote results back into the original local task and lease

That means:

- no silent remote execution
- no hidden second backlog
- no remote result that lives only in transport logs

## Bounded Surface

Shared compute is bounded by:

- allowlisted executors
- explicit working directory
- explicit timeout
- explicit target node
- explicit lane context

This is not a free-form shell bridge.

## Authority Boundary

Remote execution does not outrank local control.

The remote node may execute a bounded request.

The local colony still decides:

- whether the task was active
- which lease owned the run
- whether the result moves the task to review or blocked

That is the difference between federation and drift.

## Consequence

Shared compute is now a real execution path only when it preserves the local task/lease chain end to end.

Federation advice alone is not enough.

Federated execution without local task/lease continuity is not acceptable.

# Orientation pointer rule — noisy categories brief through role-specific packs and anchors before raw entry expansion

## Rule

When an index category becomes too large for direct orientation, the live briefing surface must compress it into role-specific pointers before widening to raw entries.

For `pattern`, that means:

1. select the role-relevant packs first
2. derive a small anchor set from those packs
3. load those anchor LX entries into the live packet before any broad type search
4. keep the rest of the category suppressed unless the mission or blockers require expansion

## Why

Truth can stay large.

Orientation cannot.

The mistake is not having a large corpus. The mistake is handing a large corpus directly to a spawned agent and pretending that is guidance.

Packs already reduce the category.

Pointers make that reduction operational by giving the role:

- a primary pack
- a small anchor chain
- an explicit rule for when to widen

## Operational Meaning

The live packet should prefer:

- pack-level orientation
- anchor LX entries
- explicit widening only when context demands it

That keeps the inherited truth intact while reducing drift and briefing noise.

## Boundary

This rule does not delete or demote canonical LX truth.

It only changes how noisy categories are surfaced at the spawn boundary.

Canonical source remains full.

Briefing surface remains compressed.

## Consequence

Noisy categories become navigable again without erasing history.

The system keeps permanent truth, but the agent receives a smaller and more role-correct entry point into that truth.

- too much noise
- weak prioritization
- poor inheritance of the right warning at the right moment

Role-specific packs keep the warning surface smaller and sharper.

- a primary mistake pack
- optional secondary packs
- a short anchor LX list
- explicit suppressed packs

Then the separate `MISTAKES TO AVOID` block should be sourced from those anchors, not from a wider generic search.

This does not reduce or delete canonical mistake entries.

It changes only the live orientation path for spawned agents.

Canonical mistake truth remains full.

Spawned warning context remains compressed.

## Consequence

Mistake guidance becomes more actionable.

Agents see the mistakes most likely to apply to their lane before they widen into the full catalog.

documents.title: Agent identity rule — stable agentId, role label, and ephemeral spawnPid must remain separate
documents.body:
# Agent identity rule — stable agentId, role label, and ephemeral spawnPid must remain separate

## Rule

Agents must carry three separate identity layers at runtime:

1. `role`
   The routing label that decides what kind of work the lane is for.
2. `agentId`
   The stable runtime identity for that agent class.
3. `spawnPid`
   The ephemeral activation instance for this specific run.

These layers must not collapse into one field.

## Responsibility Tiers

Each agent must also declare a responsibility tier.

The current tiers are:

- `observer`
- `working`
- `guard`
- `control`

Tier is part of the spawn surface because it tells the system how narrow the briefing should stay and what kind of authority the agent is allowed to exercise.

## Why

If `role`, `agentId`, and `spawnPid` collapse together, agents stop feeling temporary.

They begin to act like permanent nodes, which widens context, confuses authority, and makes despawn discipline weaker.

The system is supposed to work the opposite way:

- nodes persist
- agents activate
- leases bind work
- agents record results
- agents despawn

## Operational Meaning

Spawn packets must expose:

- `role`
- `agentId`
- `responsibilityTier`
- `lifecycle=ephemeral`
- `spawnPid`

PID registries must record the same split.

The stable identity is for orientation and policy.

The ephemeral PID is for this specific activation only.

## Boundary

This rule does not make agents permanent.

It makes agent activation more explicit and more disposable.

Persistent infrastructure remains with the node, router, colony, gateway, and ledgers.

## Consequence

Agents become easier to reason about, easier to despawn, and less likely to accumulate oversized briefings.

The control plane stays closer to the old fast model:

- compressed role packet
- stable agent identity
- ephemeral run identity
- bounded work
- mandatory despawn

documents.title: Compact runtime rule — compile validated running truth into short-code tables before machine consumption widens into markdown
documents.body:
# Compact runtime rule — compile validated running truth into short-code tables before machine consumption widens into markdown

## Rule

The validated `running` surface must be compilable into a compact machine-first runtime.

That compact runtime should expose:

- short codes for roles, tiers, and types
- entry rows with minimal machine fields
- explicit chain edges
- stable references back to the validated running signature

Agents and controllers may still use markdown canon for authoring and human review, but machine consumption should have a narrower compiled surface available first.

## Why

Markdown canon is durable and readable, but it is not the fastest runtime language.

If every machine surface expands directly from markdown, agents inherit too much prose and too little structure.

The compact runtime keeps the canonical source intact while creating a faster machine view on top of it.

## Operational Meaning

The compact runtime is:

- additive
- generated
- traceable to `running`
- never higher than canonical truth

It does not replace LX authoring.

It gives the runtime a smaller symbolic surface to read first.

## Boundary

Canonical truth still lives in:

- LX source
- validated staging/dev/running payloads
- task and lease ledgers
- ASO typed stores

The compact runtime is a derived machine surface, not a new sovereign source.

## Consequence

The system moves closer to the old fast model:

- compressed runtime packets
- smaller machine tables
- explicit chains
- stable identities
- ephemeral activations

That improves orientation speed without deleting canon.

documents.title: Tier widening rule — observer and working tiers consume compact runtime first; markdown widening is conditional
documents.body:
# Tier widening rule — observer and working tiers consume compact runtime first; markdown widening is conditional

## Rule

Lower runtime tiers must enter through the compact surface first.

For `observer` and `working` tiers, the default spawn packet should:

- load the compact runtime rows first
- keep markdown LX knowledge narrowed to the compact anchors
- defer wider markdown expansion unless the lane, mission, or blockers justify it

`guard` and `control` tiers may widen by default because their lanes coordinate boundaries and orchestration directly.

## Why

If lower tiers always receive the wider markdown packet, they stop feeling temporary and start drowning in prose.

The old fast system worked because the runtime entered through compressed chains, not long documents.

This rule restores that behavior without deleting canonical LX truth.

## Operational Meaning

Spawn packets must expose whether they are:

- `compactPreferred`
- widened or not
- why widening happened
- which LX entries were deferred

For lower tiers, widening is justified only when one of these is true:

- the lane tier defaults higher than compact-first
- mission context explicitly needs more surface
- active blockers force widening
- explicit widen mode is requested
- the compact runtime is unavailable

## Boundary

This rule does not remove markdown canon.

It changes runtime entry order:

1. compact rows and chain anchors first
2. markdown widening second, when justified

Canonical truth still remains in LX, the ledgers, ASO, and the validated promotion surfaces.

## Consequence

Lower-tier agents stay faster and less likely to get lost.

The runtime moves closer to the intended model:

- ephemeral agents
- compressed first packet
- explicit widening
- durable canon preserved

documents.title: Orchestration widening rule — live lane startup must request markdown widening explicitly for compact-first tiers
documents.body:
# Orchestration widening rule — live lane startup must request markdown widening explicitly for compact-first tiers

## Rule

At a live orchestration boundary, compact-first tiers must not widen just because a lane carries mission text.

For `observer` and `working` spawn roles started through lane-control surfaces:

- compact runtime plus anchor LX entries must remain the default
- mission text may be present without forcing widening
- markdown widening must be an explicit orchestration request

`guard` and `control` tiers may still widen by their tier default.

## Why

Lane startup is where context inflation becomes operationally dangerous.

If every lower-tier lane widens automatically whenever a controller adds mission text, compact-first runtime discipline collapses in the first real control surface.

That would recreate the old failure mode:

- too much prose
- too many inherited details
- agents losing the narrow lane

## Operational Meaning

Live lane startup surfaces must pass widening intent explicitly.

That means:

- lower-tier packets stay compact-first by default
- orchestration summaries should expose whether a packet widened
- widening should appear as a conscious control-plane decision, not a side effect of mission text

## Boundary

This rule applies to orchestration boundaries like lane startup and route-issued control surfaces.

It does not remove the ability to widen.

It requires widening to be deliberate when the receiving tier is supposed to stay narrow.

## Consequence

The compact runtime rule survives first contact with the live controller.

The system stays closer to the intended fast model:

- compact rows first
- explicit widening
- visible widening reason
- narrow lower-tier lanes
